meta.title: Bitcoin Is Just Getting Started, Says Billion Dollar Investor
meta.speakers: Moez Kassam (co-founder & CIO, Anson Funds), interviewed by Anthony Pompliano
meta.thread_line: 6 threads · trading the other side of hype · Bitcoin treasury deals · AI valuations · buying the panic (CoreWeave, Korea memory, Moderna short) · information edges · small-pond edge, activism and SPACs

snapshot: Moez Kassam runs ~$2.5-3B at **Anson Funds** and makes money by being early to a theme, then leaving when 'the music is too loud'.
Now a Bitcoin believer: Anson put ~$1B into Bitcoin treasury companies over 18 months and was a big buyer of Strive's new preferred at 90.
AI is real, but a $2T valuation for a company in the 'second, third inning' looks dot-com-like; private SPVs are 'the wild west'.
Buying the panic: record put buying (second-largest ever) with the S&P only 2% off its high; he bought CoreWeave on record puts and is going back into Korean memory.
Thinks Moderna is priced as if it cured cancer; expects selling before the trial readout.
His new edge: people trade on Claude/ChatGPT summaries of research reports, which he says miss something 75% of the time.
Stays a big fish in a small pond: $100M+ companies, long activism at $1B and below (Lionsgate), SPACs now back at trust value.

themes.title: Trade the other side of the hype: leave at the seventh inning
themes.lead: Kassam gets in as a theme starts to percolate and gets out when everyone at the party is talking about it.
bullets: Rule: if someone at a party pitches a theme and every chart is 'screaming high', ask how much is already priced in.
It's musical chairs: 'you don't have to get all the way to the ninth inning', seven innings is a good return.
Since COVID, retail is more informed and speculation rampant; GameStop and AMC taught him that things go higher and longer than you think, so size carefully.
Never picks the theme in advance (autonomous driving, crypto, cannabis); spots it as it percolates, when companies move together and deals get done.
Holding period: weeks to months, longer for bigger positions; 'singles, doubles' with a high batting average; a big day is 2-4%.
Best day ever: ~**$80M** on a National Bank of Greece recapitalisation arbitrage.
Tells companies 'we're here for a good time, not a long time': sells into strength, comes back when they need capital.

quote.text: It's not stay away from hype per se, but it's make sure you're on the other side of the hype.

themes.title: From deal flow to believer: Bitcoin, treasury companies and Strive's preferred
themes.lead: Bitcoin came to Anson as Toronto deal flow; Kassam now says it has inherent value and is 'here to stay', but late treasury companies are bad deals.
bullets: Early crypto companies listed in Toronto, where few hedge funds operate, so Anson was exposed to what became Hive and was the original fund backing Mike Novogratz's Galaxy.
Treasury-company (DAT) wave: first movers like Saylor's MicroStrategy and Vivek Ramaswamy's Strive got far better adoption; ~74 companies followed.
Anson's checks grew from $20M to $50M to ~**$1B** total over 18 months; the later and louder the music, the worse the deals.
Most treasury companies now trade below NAV, but bad covenants mean removing management costs 3-5 years of their forward earnings, wiping out the discount.
Strive's new perpetual preferred came at **90** with a ~15% yield (these usually trade at 100 with ~13%), with 18 months of payouts set aside.
Anson underwrites a ~20% IRR on 90-to-100 within about a month, then sells to retail; same playbook as Morgan Stanley's original MicroStrategy deal and Barclays.

quote.text: now I believe Bitcoin has an inherent value and it's here to stay

themes.status: AVOIDING BIG AI BETS; STRUCTURING DEALS INSTEAD
themes.title: AI is real; $2T valuations in the second inning are the problem
themes.lead: Kassam calls AI disruption '100% legit' but won't bet on picking the winner at today's prices.
bullets: It changed his life: he set up ChatGPT's new agent to read his parents' email and calendar.
Dot-com parallel: everyone backed Yahoo, Excite and AOL, and the eventual winner 'came out of nowhere'.
The Nvidia / data-center / chip ecosystem is 'one big circle' of related-party deals, which makes him reserved.
Can't say whether Anthropic 'or whomever' wins; Pompliano notes Anthropic's tokenized price fell from ~$2T to ~$1.6T in two weeks.
Private markets are 'the wild west': layers of SPVs charging '1 and 10' or '2 and 20'; 95% of people who say they own a stake aren't on the cap table.
Anthropic has been more prudent with its structured holdings than OpenAI and others.

themes.title: Zag when they zig: CoreWeave puts, Korean memory and Moderna's cancer hype
themes.lead: When the puts pile up he buys; when retail prices in a miracle he sells.
bullets: Pompliano: S&P only 2% off its all-time high, yet people predicted a repeat of Black Monday (Oct 19, 1987); Friday was the **second-largest** put buying ever, Nasdaq the third.
CoreWeave: Citadel Securities told him Thursday they'd never seen so much put buying; Anson bought, it ripped, and he sold when everyone wanted back in.
Korea is 'the engine' of the AI trade: Samsung and SK Hynix control memory; Samsung just posted the **largest quarterly earnings in history**.
Memory went boom to bust; now that everyone has 'thrown in the towel' he's buying for a 10-15% jump in days or weeks, not the long game.
Moderna is up ~100% on a cancer-trial headline with no efficacy data yet; readout due in about 10 days.
Biotech specialists have been burned shorting it; his call is 'buy on rumor, sell on news', with selling starting days before the readout.

quote.text: It's for sure worth more than that point, but it's probably not worth another 100%.

themes.watch: He admits he has no edge on cancer efficacy data or on trillion-dollar Korean names; both calls are sentiment reads, and he plays expected value, not certainty.

themes.title: Trading the robots: LLM summaries, prediction markets and night-time dislocations
themes.lead: Kassam's edge is watching how everyone else reacts, and more of them now react to an AI summary.
bullets: Nobody reads short or buy reports anymore; they paste them into Claude or ChatGPT and trade the summary. He finds it misses something **75%** of the time and gets it wholly wrong 10-15%.

Prediction markets: 'better than polling data'; bettors often have real-world information (Pompliano's example: a Tesla windshield supplier betting on deliveries). Anson uses them as one variable but doesn't bet.
Big funds model Apple from every chip supplier, even Tim Cook's movements; he doesn't compete there, he watches the output.
In-house software tracks positive vs. negative retail chatter per name and flags divergences; Anson doesn't post on social media (SEC and Canadian rules).
Pre-listing and overnight markets (e.g. SpaceX and SK Hynix before listing): margin stop-losses can knock names down 10-15% in an hour; traders cover 4am to 7pm.
Pod structure with sizing limits; above them traders call him, three or four times a night; a six-screen Bloomberg sits two feet from his bed.
Won't compete with Ken Griffin's Citadel on automated trading; Pompliano cites a hedge-fund line about a London poker player waking early to play drunk East Coast players.

quote.text: I think my job and our returns are going to actually get better because everyone else is becoming effectively a robot.

themes.watch: The 75% figure is his own estimate from his desk, not a study.

themes.title: Big fish, small pond: activism, SPACs and a Toronto base
themes.lead: Kassam deliberately stays small enough to play where big funds' screens can't reach.
bullets: Big funds screen for >$5-10B market caps or $100M a day; Anson looks at $100M+ companies with at least $4-5M per position, up to $100M checks.
Made ~$3B while raising almost nothing: net redemptions every year, no marketing; at their size a 10% return is hundreds of millions.
Single-name shorting faded: 'most people who short are gone' in a perennial bull market; managers buy puts or short baskets instead.

Long activism at $1B and below with fragmented retail holders: wins in Canadian REITs and Clear Channel; now in a campaign pushing Lionsgate toward a sale as studios consolidate around Netflix and streamers.
SPACs: Russell/IWM momentum names are down 20-25% while the S&P sits near highs, so SPACs fell back to trust value; downside is limited, so banks lend against them.
Buying SPACs with big sponsors like Michael Klein's.

Toronto is an edge: off the 'circus', on Bay Street in the Brookfield building with 90% of trades in the US; returning expats are easy hires, and new industries (cannabis, crypto) list in Canada first.

takeaways.title: Exit a theme when it's party talk and every chart is vertical; aim for seven innings, not nine.
Read record put buying near all-time highs as fuel for a squeeze, not a crash signal.
Avoid late-cycle Bitcoin treasury companies; if you want exposure, look at discounted new preferreds, not the 74th copycat.
Read the source report yourself; an LLM summary is what the crowd trades on, and it often misses things.
Separate hope from price in emotional stocks: ask what's priced in before a binary readout.
Fish where big funds can't: sub-$1B names with fragmented retail holders.

claims.claim: Moderna sells off into its cancer-trial readout, with selling starting before the data, due in about 10 days.
Korean memory names jump 10-15% in days or weeks as markets stabilise.
Strive's new perpetual preferred rises from 90 to par (100) within about a month, a ~20% IRR.
Bitcoin rises 30-50% over the next year in the model investors are underwriting.
After the second-largest put buying in history, the market goes up and forces short cover rather than crashing.

relations.note: large buyer of its new perpetual preferred

other_news.title: **Space:** a big theme but 'everyone gets way too excited too early'; Anson underwrote a couple of names but says you can't put 10% of your money there.

**Tesla:** never shorted it, calls it a technology company (batteries, then autonomy), but valuations are 'pretty deep' and he has no edge; skips SpaceX-Tesla merger arbitrage for the same reason. Drives a convertible Mini Cooper.

**Olympic 'great to gold' fund:** with partner Adrian, Kassam funds last-mile coaching and gear for Canadian athletes (many live on ~$18-20K a year); they backed 10% of athletes and got 30% of the medals, then repeated it at the Winter Games.
**Canada-US:** amid the trade war he says Canada doesn't want to join the US and both are better as friends; Kevin O'Leary is his neighbour in Muskoka.
**Downside of democratised trading:** retail thinks it has more edge than it does; funds are 'like the casino' and most players leave poorer.

Pompliano's Elliott story: seizing an Argentine navy ship as collateral on defaulted bonds bought at ~25 cents; Kassam says the story is 'more nuanced' and Anson won't go that far. Elliott and Starboard named as large activists.

Sources referenced: Citadel Securities (CoreWeave put flow), a Ken Griffin-attributed poker anecdote, Michael Burry (Pompliano: 'a Substack writer'). Kassam is on Instagram as Munching Moez (food and fun).

glossary.def: Digital asset treasury company: a listed company that raises capital mainly to hold crypto such as Bitcoin.
Preferred stock with no maturity paying a fixed dividend; treasury companies use it for levered Bitcoin exposure.
A security's face value (100); a preferred issued at 90 offers upside as it moves toward par.
Special-purpose vehicle pooling investors into one private stake, often layered with extra fees.
The cash per share held in a SPAC's trust, which caps the downside before a deal.
Buying a stake and pushing management (buybacks, asset sales, a sale of the company) to lift the price.
